cap:
Posting by hand every day is a time trap.

Queue your posts in a Google Sheet and let a daily automation publish the next one. You only review.

h: AI Won't Fix A Bad Process
cap:
AI on top of a messy process just makes the mess faster.

Map it, simplify it, then automate it.

Your first Make scenario is three moves.

A trigger, a few modules and a test run. Start small and build from there.

Do not know where to begin?

These three are simple, useful and low-risk. Pick one this week.

Weak prompts give weak results.

Tell the AI who it is, what format you want and show one example.

You do not need a heavy CRM on day one.

A Google Sheet plus a simple automation can track every lead.

There is no single best tool.

Choose by complexity, who maintains it and where your data must live. Check current pricing before deciding.

Automation is only worth it if it gives time back.

Start with the task you repeat most and measure the result.

AI drafts fast, but it can be wrong.

Keep a quick human review before anything goes public.

A webhook is a doorbell for your automation.

An app rings it with data and your scenario starts running.

Put a filter right after your trigger.

Unwanted bundles stop early, so you keep your operations for real work.

Every automation will fail one day.

Pick the right error handler per step so one failure does not break everything.

pts: Tags not related to the post
cap:
More hashtags is not better hashtags.

Keep them relevant and rotate your sets.

Most leads go quiet because nobody follows up.

A simple rule-based nudge fixes that.

A content calendar that runs itself is possible.

Topics in a Sheet, AI drafts, your approval and a daily publish.

Do not turn an automation on and hope.

Test it with sample data and read every module output.

Stop creating from zero every day.

Turn one idea into five formats and share it across the week.

The same person can fill your form three times.

Clean the email and search first, so you keep one record.

pts: It is not only for big companies
cap:
Automation is useful for small teams too.

But it needs a clear process and a little maintenance.

Use AI to plan and Make to run.

Describe the outcome, build the scenario, test it and refine.

Use the same prompt skeleton every time.

Role, audience, format and banned words give far more consistent posts.

pts: A new Sheet row starts it
cap:
A great first build.

Idea in a Sheet, AI draft out, saved in the same row for review.

Copying data between apps is pure repetition.

Connect them once and let the data move on its own.

Reviews build trust, but people rarely remember to leave them.

A polite automated request fixes that.

Consistency beats random posting.

Choose a time your audience is active and confirm the timezone.

If you cannot see failures, you cannot fix them.

Log every error to a Sheet and review it each week.

AI can draft replies in seconds.

Give it your real FAQs and keep a human on the send button.

Batching turns daily stress into one focused hour.

Write once, queue it and let automation publish.

Small businesses gain a lot from simple automations.

Start with the messages you send again and again.

Three questions save you hours of rebuilding.

If you cannot answer them, fix the process first.

Retries should never create duplicates.

Check before you write and update the status only after the action succeeds.

A 429 error means slow down.

Space out your calls and let failed bundles retry later.

pts: Data store is for the machine
cap:
Both hold rows, but they serve different jobs.

Use Sheets for people and a Data store for scenario state.

pts: Each item runs on its own
cap:
An Iterator turns one bundle into many.

Without an Aggregator later, your operations can grow fast.

Use a Router when the same data needs different treatment.

Always keep a fallback so nothing silently disappears.

Know what uses your operations.

Every module run per bundle counts, so design with bundle counts in mind.

A public webhook URL is an open door.

Check a secret token at the start of the scenario.

JSON is how apps and AI talk to each other.

Learn these three basics and automation gets much easier.

Free-text AI output breaks scenarios.

Ask for strict JSON and validate it before the next module.

One prompt, one job.

Chain small steps so each one is easy to test and improve.

Posting to Instagram through automation has rules.

You need a Business or Creator account linked to a Facebook Page and a public image link.

A reliable LinkedIn flow is simple.

Queue, caption, image and a log of what was posted.

Add one status column and keep control.

Automation publishes only what you approved.

The first line decides whether people keep reading.

Name the problem and promise a fix.

A post without a call to action leaves reach on the table.

End with one clear, easy ask.

A lead magnet does not need to be big.

One useful checklist, delivered automatically, can start your list.

Let AI sort the inbox.

Use fixed categories and keep a review path for unclear emails.

Wrong posting times are usually a timezone issue.

Format dates with a clear timezone and test around midnight.

Stop rebuilding the same report.

Let automation gather the data and AI draft the summary.

Order matters.

Map first, simplify second and automate last.

Measure whether automation really paid off.

Include maintenance time in your numbers, not only the build.

AI services can fail or hit limits.

Give every AI step a plan B so the workflow still finishes.

Better image prompts give better visuals.

Describe the subject, the scene and the light in clear words.

Default module names become a puzzle later.

Rename them by purpose and leave short notes.

Sudden 401 and 403 errors usually mean login problems.

Check token expiry and that every needed permission was ticked.

Most random failures come from messy input.

Clean the data before you write it anywhere.

Big plans stall. Small wins compound.

Automate one task well before adding the next.

Ask what matters most before picking a tool.

Complexity, maintenance and data rules decide more than hype.

A simple 30-day path.

Map, build, test and measure. Small steps, steady progress.

Automation is a habit, not a one-time project.

One small improvement a week adds up fast.
